title: Structure and Liftoff In Combustion Experiment

sources.title: Structure and Liftoff In Combustion Experiment
A Computational and Experimental Study of Coflow Laminar Methane/Air Diffusion Flames: Effects of Fuel Dilution, Inlet Velocity, and Gravity

key_findings: The structure and stability of laminar diffusion flames in microgravity are significantly influenced by burner diameter, coflow velocity, and fuel composition.
The liftoff velocity limits for different fuels and burner diameters were determined.
Fuel dilution with nitrogen impacted soot formation and flame stability.
fields.earth_applications: Improved numerical models for flame behavior lead to more efficient combustion technologies on Earth.

paper_findings.text: Computed temperature profiles accurately modeled the shapes and magnitudes of measured temperature profiles.
The influences of varying inlet velocity were correctly captured.
As gravity is eliminated, the discrepancy between computed and measured flame lengths decreased.

conditions.label: CH4-air diffusion flames under microgravity
evidence: A series of nitrogen-diluted flames measured in the Structure and Liftoﬀ in Combustion Experiment (SLICE) on board the International Space Station was assessed numerically under microgravity (μg) and normal gravity (1g) conditions with CH4 mole fraction ranging from 0.4 to 1.0 and average inlet velocity ranging from 23 to 90 cm/s.

conditions.label: CH4-air diffusion flames under normal gravity
evidence: A series of nitrogen-diluted flames measured in the Structure and Liftoﬀ in Combustion Experiment (SLICE) on board the International Space Station was assessed numerically under microgravity (μg) and normal gravity (1g) conditions with CH4 mole fraction ranging from 0.4 to 1.0 and average inlet velocity ranging from 23 to 90 cm/s.

key_findings: Computed temperature profiles accurately modeled the shapes and magnitudes of measured temperature profiles.
The influences of varying inlet velocity were correctly captured.
As gravity is eliminated, the discrepancy between computed and measured flame lengths decreased.
